scenes.headline: Four benchmark claims, read against the boards
scenes.sub: What a security model's launch numbers measure
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Caliper! Today: a security model launched with four big benchmark numbers, and what each one really measures.

scenes.text: A benchmark score is only as good as its denominator and its conditions. Here the best-checked number measures a two-model system, not the model being launched.
scenes.say: A score is only as good as what it counts. Here the one number you can check measures a two-model system, not the model being launched.

steps.say: A cheap worker model runs every one of the tasks, and its answer goes to the grader.
When it stalls, a router hands the hard case to the specialist. That happened on fewer than half the tasks.

scenes.title: CyberGym, level 1
scenes.say: The same worker model scores ninety four in someone else's agent, and under seventy seven in its maker's own. The agent around a model moves the score more than the model.

left.title: As launched
left.say: As launched, the numbers are thirty nine of thirty nine, and twenty three of twenty four.

right.title: Over every task
right.say: But Cybench has forty tasks, and CVE-Bench forty. Nobody says which were left out, or why.

steps.say: And these tasks were public long before today's models were trained, many with solution scripts beside them.

scenes.text: For a model sold on finding real vulnerabilities, the launch gives nothing checkable about the model itself.
scenes.mark: nothing checkable about the model itself
scenes.say: For a model sold on finding real vulnerabilities, the bar should be higher, not lower: run settings, the excluded tasks, and someone else's evaluation.
Check the denominator. Ask who ran the tasks. And remember the tasks are older than the models.
